title: Robust topological oscillators govern a tunable phase transition to synchronized circadian rhythms
authors: Chongbin Zheng, Evelyn Tang, Peter Thomas
abstract: While synchronization has been well-studied in deterministic oscillators, most underlying oscillators are stochastic in both natural and man-made systems. Yet, the effects of intrinsic stochasticity remain poorly understood. Here, we develop a new mechanism for synchronizing circadian KaiC molecules that have topologically protected cycles. We find a phase transition to synchronization that depends only on the single-oscillator coherence, across a range of molecular changes that determine this coherence. Examining both mesoscopic and macroscopic numbers relevant for cellular and in vitro conditions respectively, we find different scaling properties above and below the phase transition. Our results shed light on several existing experiments and further predict that external changes can be offset by compensatory changes that improve the single-oscillator coherence - demonstrating a tunable pathway between stochastic single oscillators and their robust collective rhythms.
summary: This work develops a theoretical model for circadian rhythm synchronization in biological oscillators that incorporate intrinsic noise. It establishes that the transition to robust, synchronized rhythms is governed solely by the single-oscillator coherence ($R_1$). The findings provide a powerful framework for understanding how molecular parameters can be tuned to maintain collective order despite underlying stochasticity.
main_problem: The research aims to understand how intrinsic stochastic noise affects synchronization in biological oscillators, particularly developing a tunable mechanism for achieving robust collective rhythms.
main_result: Synchronization is shown to depend only on the single-oscillator coherence ($R_1$), leading to a phase transition predicted at $R_1 \gtrsim 1.96$, independent of specific biochemical rates.
method: The study uses stochastic modeling (master equation) and analyzes both mesoscopic and macroscopic limits, characterizing dynamics via coherence measures and scaling laws around the critical point.
model_or_system: The system models the KaiABC circadian clock in cyanobacteria, focusing on the phosphorylation of KaiC proteins. The dynamics are governed by rate equations incorporating coupling strength derived from KaiA sequestration.
key_observables: Single-oscillator coherence ($R_1$), population-level coherence ($R_N$), and timing error (coefficient of variation of the period $T$).
important_parameters: Topological parameter ($ho$), thermodynamic force ($\mu$, related to ATP/ADP ratio), and coupling strength ($c_{seq}A$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling stochastic transitions, using a diffusion approximation for large N, and assuming instantaneous KaiA sequestration upon entering specific state regions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the single-molecule phase space, population synchronization dynamics showing scaling laws above/below the transition, and how experimental modifications tune parameters leading to changes in collective behavior.
paper_structure: The paper develops a novel mechanism linking synchronization to $R_1$, analyzes the resulting phase transition using deterministic limits, examines mesoscopic vs. macroscopic scaling properties, and discusses compensatory mechanisms that restore coherence after disruption.
why_interesting: While focused on biology, the mathematical framework—analyzing phase transitions in coupled stochastic systems based on a single-particle metric ($R_1$)—is highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and open quantum systems exhibiting collective behavior.
